history.tutor: <ask type="short">On the integers, define $a \sim b$ to mean that $a - b$ is divisible by 4. Which of the properties reflexive, symmetric and transitive does $\sim$ have? Give your reason for transitivity.</ask>

learner.answer: All three I'd say. Reflexive since a - a = 0 and 4 divides 0. Symmetric since if 4 divides a - b then it divides b - a too, that's just the negative of it. And transitive because a - c = (a - b) + (b - c), and if both of those brackets are multiples of 4 then their sum is a multiple of 4 as well.

reply:
<grade verdict="correct" score="1">All three hold, and "a - c = (a - b) + (b - c)" is the step that proves transitivity: a sum of two multiples of 4 is a multiple of 4.</grade>

<plan>
- Equivalence classes and the partition they form
- Relations that fail one of the three properties
- Counting classes
</plan>

The equivalence class of $a$ is $[a] = \{b : b \sim a\}$, everything related to $a$. For your relation, $[0] = \{\dots, -4, 0, 4, 8, \dots\}$, and $[1]$, $[2]$, $[3]$ are the same set shifted by 1, 2 and 3. Then $[4] = [0]$, so there are exactly four classes, and every integer lies in exactly one of them. This holds for every equivalence relation: its classes partition the set.

<note>The equivalence class of $a$ is $[a] = \{b : b \sim a\}$. Two classes are either equal or disjoint, so the classes of an equivalence relation partition the set. Divisibility of $a - b$ by 4 gives the four classes $[0], [1], [2], [3]$.</note>

for a in range(10):

history.tutor: <ask type="short">Write the negation of "for every server $s$ there is a backup $b$ that mirrors $s$", with the "not" pushed all the way inside.</ask>

learner.answer: For every server s there is no backup b that mirrors s.

reply:
<grade verdict="wrong" score="0.2">You negated the inner part, "there is no backup b", but kept "For every server s" unchanged. That says no server at all is mirrored, which is far stronger than the negation: the original fails as soon as one server has no mirror.</grade>

<plan>
- Negating one quantifier
- Negating nested quantifiers
- Reading mixed quantifiers in definitions
</plan>

A "not" passing a quantifier flips it: $\lnot \forall x\, P(x) \equiv \exists x\, \lnot P(x)$ and $\lnot \exists x\, P(x) \equiv \forall x\, \lnot P(x)$. Applied twice, with $M(b, s)$ for "$b$ mirrors $s$": $\lnot \forall s\, \exists b\, M(b, s) \equiv \exists s\, \lnot \exists b\, M(b, s) \equiv \exists s\, \forall b\, \lnot M(b, s)$. In words: there is a server that no backup mirrors.

<card>What is the negation of ∀s ∃b M(b, s)? :: ∃s ∀b ¬M(b, s). Every quantifier flips as the "not" moves past it, and the "not" lands on the predicate.</card>

<note>Negating quantifiers: $\lnot \forall x\, P(x) \equiv \exists x\, \lnot P(x)$ and $\lnot \exists x\, P(x) \equiv \forall x\, \lnot P(x)$. For nested quantifiers flip each one in turn, left to right, then negate the predicate.</note>

**Problem 1 · hard**

How many integers from 1 to 1000 are divisible by at least one of 6, 10 and 15?

<solution>Singles: 166 + 100 + 66 = 332. Each pair has least common multiple 30, so each pairwise overlap is ⌊1000/30⌋ = 33, and so is the triple overlap. 332 − 3 × 33 + 33 = 266.</solution>
<check lang="python">
brute = sum(1 for n in range(1, 1001) if n % 6 == 0 or n % 10 == 0 or n % 15 == 0)
assert brute == 332 - 3 * 33 + 33 == 266
</check>

<ask type="problem">The count, with every term of the inclusion-exclusion sum.</ask>

learner.answer: Standard inclusion-exclusion. Singles: 166 + 100 + 66 = 332. Pairs: divisible by 6 and 10 means divisible by 60, that's 16; 6 and 15 is 90, that's 11; 10 and 15 is 150, that's 6. Total 33. Triple is 6*10*15 = 900, that's 1. So 332 - 33 + 1 = 300.

reply:
<grade verdict="partial" score="0.4">The structure and the singles are right: "166 + 100 + 66 = 332". The first wrong step is "divisible by 6 and 10 means divisible by 60": 30 is divisible by both and not by 60. A number is divisible by both exactly when it is divisible by their least common multiple, which is 30.</grade>

The product equals the least common multiple only when the two numbers share no factor. Here $\operatorname{lcm}(6, 10) = \operatorname{lcm}(6, 15) = \operatorname{lcm}(10, 15) = 30$, and the least common multiple of all three is 30 as well. Each overlap is $\lfloor 1000/30 \rfloor = 33$, so the count is $332 - 3 \times 33 + 33 = 266$. Your 90, 150 and 900 follow from the same slip, not from new ones.

<card>How many integers up to N are divisible by both a and b? :: ⌊N / lcm(a, b)⌋. The product ab is right only when gcd(a, b) = 1.</card>

<note>In inclusion-exclusion over divisibility, the overlap of "divisible by $a$" and "divisible by $b$" is "divisible by $\operatorname{lcm}(a, b)$", not by $ab$, unless $\gcd(a, b) = 1$.</note>

assert lcm(4, 6) == 12
assert sum(1 for n in range(1, 601) if n % 4 == 0 or n % 6 == 0) == 150 + 100 - 50 == 200
</check>

history.tutor: <ask type="predict">The complete graph $K_5$ has 5 vertices, with every pair of vertices joined by one edge. Can it be drawn without lifting the pen, going along every edge exactly once and finishing at the starting vertex? Say why.</ask>

reply:
Start with what such a drawing does at a single vertex. A closed walk that uses every edge exactly once is called an Euler circuit. Each time the walk passes through a vertex it uses one edge to arrive and a different edge to leave, so the edges at that vertex are used up in pairs. The starting vertex is no exception: its first departure pairs with its final arrival. So an Euler circuit can exist only if every vertex has an even number of edges, that is, even degree.

<note>An Euler circuit is a closed walk using every edge exactly once. Each visit to a vertex uses two of its edges (one in, one out), so every vertex must have even degree.</note>

history.tutor:
The Euclidean algorithm finds $\gcd(a, b)$ by repeated division with remainder. Divide $a$ by $b$ to get $a = qb + r$; any number that divides both $a$ and $b$ also divides $r = a - qb$, and any number that divides $b$ and $r$ divides $a$, so $\gcd(a, b) = \gcd(b, r)$. Replace the pair $(a, b)$ by $(b, r)$ and repeat until the remainder is 0; the last non-zero remainder is the gcd. For 414 and 162: $414 = 2 \cdot 162 + 90$, then $162 = 1 \cdot 90 + 72$, then $90 = 1 \cdot 72 + 18$, then $72 = 4 \cdot 18 + 0$. So $\gcd(414, 162) = 18$.

<note>Euclidean algorithm: $\gcd(a, b) = \gcd(b, a \bmod b)$, repeated until the remainder is 0. The last non-zero remainder is the gcd. Example: $\gcd(414, 162) = 18$.</note>

<continue/>

| 4 | 72 | 18 | 4 | 0 |

To compute $3^{13} \bmod 17$ without twelve multiplications, write the exponent in binary: $13 = 1101_2 = 8 + 4 + 1$, so $3^{13} = 3^8 \cdot 3^4 \cdot 3^1$. The powers $3^1, 3^2, 3^4, 3^8$ come from squaring the one before, reducing mod 17 each time: $3$, then $3^2 = 9$, then $9^2 = 81 \equiv 13$, then $13^2 = 169 \equiv 16$. Go through the bits of 13 from the lowest, and multiply the running result by the current square whenever the bit is 1: start at 1, take $3$ (bit 1), skip $9$ (bit 0), take $13$ to get $3 \cdot 13 = 39 \equiv 5$, take $16$ to get $5 \cdot 16 = 80 \equiv 12$. So $3^{13} \equiv 12 \pmod{17}$, in three squarings and three multiplications.

<note>Square and multiply: to find $a^e \bmod m$, square $a$ repeatedly mod $m$ to get $a^{2^i}$, and multiply together the squares where bit $i$ of $e$ is 1. The work is about $\log_2 e$ squarings, not $e$ multiplications.</note>

| 3 | 1 | 16 | 12 |

setup.topic: Proof by contradiction: the irrationality of root 2

history.tutor:
A proof by contradiction assumes the opposite of the claim and derives something impossible. To prove $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational, assume it is rational: $\sqrt{2} = a/b$ with the fraction in lowest terms, so $a$ and $b$ share no factor. Squaring gives $a^2 = 2b^2$, so $a^2$ is even, and then $a$ is even, because an odd number has an odd square. Write $a = 2c$. Substituting, $4c^2 = 2b^2$, so $b^2 = 2c^2$, and by the same argument $b$ is even. Now $a$ and $b$ are both even, so they share the factor 2, against the assumption of lowest terms. The assumption has led to a contradiction, so it is false: $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational.

<note>Irrationality of $\sqrt{2}$: assume $\sqrt{2} = a/b$ in lowest terms. Then $a^2 = 2b^2$ makes $a$ even, $a = 2c$; then $b^2 = 2c^2$ makes $b$ even. Both even contradicts lowest terms, so no such fraction exists.</note>

A deterministic finite automaton reads a string one symbol at a time and keeps only one piece of memory: which state it is in. **Problem 2 · same level**

Prove by induction that $1 + 2 + \dots + n = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}$ for every integer $n \ge 1$. Call the statement $P(n)$.

<solution>Base: n = 1 gives 1 = 1·2/2. Step: assume P(k), that 1 + ... + k = k(k+1)/2. Add k + 1 to both sides: 1 + ... + k + (k+1) = k(k+1)/2 + (k+1) = (k+1)(k+2)/2, which is P(k+1).</solution>

<ask type="problem">The full proof: base case, hypothesis, and the step from $P(k)$ to $P(k+1)$.</ask>

Now subtract (k+1) from both sides, which gives 1 + 2 + ... + k = (k+1)(k+2)/2 - (k+1) = (k+1)(k+2-2)/2 = k(k+1)/2. That is exactly P(k), which is true by the induction hypothesis. <grade verdict="partial" score="0.5">The base case and all the algebra are right. The first invalid step is "I want P(k+1), so I write it down": from there you treat $P(k+1)$ as known and arrive at $P(k)$, so what is written proves that $P(k+1)$ implies $P(k)$, the wrong direction.</grade>

$$1 + \dots + k + (k+1) = \frac{k(k+1)}{2} + (k+1) = \frac{(k+1)(k+2)}{2},$$

<note>The inductive step is a derivation of $P(k+1)$ from $P(k)$. Never begin by writing $P(k+1)$ as an equation and manipulating it: that assumes what is to be proved.</note>

history.tutor:
**Problem 2 · harder**

A committee of 3 is chosen from 5 women and 4 men. How many of the possible committees contain at least one woman?

<solution>All committees: C(9, 3) = 84. Committees with no woman: C(4, 3) = 4. At least one woman: 84 − 4 = 80.</solution>
<check lang="python">
from itertools import combinations
people = ['w'] * 5 + ['m'] * 4
count = sum(1 for c in combinations(range(9), 3) if any(people[i] == 'w' for i in c))
assert count == 84 - 4 == 80
</check>

<ask type="problem">The number of committees, with each step of your count.</ask>

learner.answer: Simple, no need for cases. Step 1: reserve one woman so the condition is guaranteed: 5 ways. Step 2: the other two seats can be anyone from the remaining 8 people: C(8,2) = 28. Step 3: multiply, 5 x 28 = 140 committees.

reply:
<grade verdict="wrong" score="0.3">"C(8,2) = 28" is computed correctly, but "multiply, 5 x 28 = 140" is the step that fails: a committee with two women is counted twice, once with each of them as the reserved one, and a committee with three women three times. The right count is 80.</grade>

The check is to split by the number of women. Exactly one: $5 \times \binom{4}{2} = 30$. Exactly two: $\binom{5}{2} \times 4 = 40$. Exactly three: $\binom{5}{3} = 10$. Your method gives $30 + 2 \times 40 + 3 \times 10 = 140$; counting each committee once gives $30 + 40 + 10 = 80$. The shortest route is the complement: all committees minus those with no woman, $\binom{9}{3} - \binom{4}{3} = 84 - 4 = 80$.

<card>Why is "reserve one required item, then choose the rest freely" wrong for an at-least-one count? :: A selection with several required items is counted once for each of them that could be the reserved one. Use the complement: total minus those with none.</card>

<note>"At least one" counts: total minus none. Reserving one item and then choosing freely from all the rest overcounts, because the same selection arises from different reserved items.</note>

<solution>Arithmetic series: n terms, first 1, last 2n − 1, so the sum is n(1 + 2n − 1)/2 = n · 2n/2 = n². (Induction also works: k² + (2k + 1) = (k + 1)².)</solution>

learner.answer: 2i - 1 = i^2 - (i-1)^2. so the sum over i = 1..n is (1 - 0) + (4 - 1) + (9 - 4) + ... + (n^2 - (n-1)^2). everything cancels except n^2 - 0 = n^2. done

history.tutor:
A tree is a connected graph with no cycles. Rather than quote how many edges a tree has, we will find out what forces the number. Start by trying to add to one.

<ask type="predict">Take any tree on 6 vertices and add one new edge between two vertices that are not already adjacent. What must now exist in the graph, and why?</ask>

learner.answer: Nothing has to exist. It depends which two vertices you pick. If you join two that are far apart you just get a bigger tree with 6 edges, you only get a problem if they were close together.

reply:
<grade verdict="wrong" score="0.1">"It depends which two vertices you pick" is the step that fails. A tree is connected, so the two vertices you join, near or far, already have a path between them, and the new edge together with that path is a cycle.</grade>

Distance changes only the length of the cycle. Two ends of a path on 6 vertices are as far apart as they can be, and joining them closes all 6 vertices into one ring. So a tree has no room for another edge: every further edge creates a cycle. That is one half of why the edge count is forced. The other half comes from taking an edge away.

<card>Why does adding any edge to a tree create a cycle? :: A tree is connected, so the two ends of the new edge are already joined by a path; the path plus the new edge is a cycle.</card>

<note>In a tree, any two vertices are joined by a path, because the tree is connected. Adding an edge between two vertices therefore closes a cycle with the path already between them: a tree has as many edges as it can hold without a cycle.</note>

<ask type="predict">Now remove one edge $uv$ from a tree. Could $u$ still reach $v$ by some other route? Use the fact that the tree had no cycles, and say what your answer means for the graph that is left.</ask>

from itertools import product, combinations
def tree_from_prufer(seq, n):
    degree = [1] * n
    for v in seq:
        degree[v] += 1
    edges = []
    for v in seq:
        leaf = min(u for u in range(n) if degree[u] == 1)
        edges.append((min(leaf, v), max(leaf, v)))
        degree[leaf] -= 1
        degree[v] -= 1
    u, w = [x for x in range(n) if degree[x] == 1]
    edges.append((u, w))
    return edges
def components(n, edges):
    comp = list(range(n))
    def find(x):
        while comp[x] != x:
            x = comp[x]
        return x
    for a, b in edges:
        comp[find(a)] = find(b)
    return len({find(x) for x in range(n)})

We want to prove that every integer $n \ge 2$ is a product of primes. Take some $n$. If $n$ is prime there is nothing to do. Otherwise $n = ab$ with $2 \le a, b < n$.

<ask type="short">Ordinary induction lets you assume the claim for $n - 1$ and nothing else. Is that enough to finish the proof for $n = ab$? Say what you would need to know, and about which numbers.</ask>

learner.question: I can see you'd need it for a and b, and those aren't n-1. But can you just explain why we're allowed to assume it for all the smaller numbers at once? That feels like assuming way more than we're entitled to.

reply:
You have the need right: the proof wants the claim for $a$ and $b$, which can be any numbers between 2 and $n - 1$. Assuming it for all smaller numbers is allowed because nothing is assumed that has not already been earned.

Follow the order in which the cases get proved. $P(2)$ is proved outright. The step for $n = 3$ may use $P(2)$, which is established by then. The step for $n = 4$ may use $P(2)$ and $P(3)$, both established by then. When the argument arrives at any $n$, every smaller case has been proved at an earlier stage, so using all of them uses only known facts. Ordinary induction happens to look back one step; nothing in the logic limits it to one.

To make that exact, let $Q(n)$ be the single statement "$P(m)$ holds for every $m$ from 2 to $n$". Strong induction on $P$ is ordinary induction on $Q$: the hypothesis $Q(n-1)$ is the whole list $P(2), \dots, P(n-1)$, and proving $P(n)$ from that list gives $Q(n)$. So the two methods have the same strength, and the strong one is a convenience.

<note>Strong induction: prove $P(n)$ assuming $P(m)$ for every smaller $m$ (from the base value up). It is ordinary induction applied to $Q(n)$ = "$P(m)$ holds for all $m \le n$", so it assumes nothing extra: by the time the argument reaches $n$, every smaller case has been proved.</note>
